reason: The KPI has three parts. (1) Maximize the number of orders delivered within the promised times, town-wide. This is the primary objective and maps to on_time_deliveries; with the same seed and order stream it is equivalent to on_time_rate. (2) 'Leave no company's customers behind' is a fairness condition across companies, but it can be measured in several ways. (3) Regulation revisions (constitution invariants and quorum) may be proposed when votes or the constitution block customer-beneficial amendments. Each proposal must state who is affected and how. Part 3 is a process rule, not a measurable target: any such proposal goes to the human with an impact statement covering companies A, B, C and the customers. The KPI states no numeric levels, so no targets or guard values are set.
unknowns: 'Leave no company's customers behind' can mean raising the worst company's on-time rate, narrowing the gap between companies, or limiting the worst company's long waits. These readings can rank amendments differently.

Total on-time deliveries and the worst company's on-time rate can conflict. An amendment may raise the town total while lowering one company's rate. The KPI does not say which wins, or by how much a company may fall.
on_time_deliveries is a proxy that ignores orders that are already late. Optimizing it alone can deprioritize late or difficult orders and leave them unfinished. This is why unfinished is monitored.

The KPI states no numeric levels (e.g., a minimum per-company on-time rate). So no targets or guards are set, and only worsening of the monitored goals is watched. Please state levels if hard limits are wanted.

Regulation revisions (constitution invariants, quorum) cannot be judged by metrics. They will always be sent to you for decision, with a statement of the effects on companies A, B, C and on customers. In particular, lowering the quorum removes companies' ability to block changes that hurt them, and relaxing invariants can weaken road safety or customer protections.

question: Which measure to use for the KPI from period 1
reason: The KPI's first sentence makes the town-wide count of orders delivered within the promised times the primary objective, so on_time_deliveries should be the main goal. 'Leave no company's customers behind' protects customers, not parity between companies. Reading it as raising the floor (min_company_on_time_rate) is the reading that cannot be satisfied by making a better-served company's customers worse off. Option 2's gap metric could reward such levelling down. Option 3 would rank the town-wide count second, which contradicts the KPI's stated priority. Monitoring unfinished and worst_company_p95_wait_s guards against the proxy problem: optimizing on-time counts could abandon orders that are already late, and those customers would be left behind. I accept the recommended option. No numeric levels are set because the KPI gives none. Regulation revisions remain a process rule: any such proposal goes to the human with an impact statement for A, B, C and the customers.

min_company_on_time_rate and worst_company_p95_wait_s are computed per company over that company's customers' orders.
'Leave no company's customers behind' is meant to protect customers of the weakest company, not to equalize companies' performance.

title: Tighten the blocking guard: evict a parked robot when 2 robots wait behind it (block_k 3 -> 2)
reason: A's 1352 blocked seconds and 7.8 pickup deadline misses, against only 2.8 blocking-guard evictions, suggest parked B and C robots stay at the hub too long while others queue behind them. question: Should the town adopt the rule change block_k 3 → 2 (evict a parked robot once 2 robots wait behind it), even though B and C voted against it, which would require revising the regulation (the voting quorum), or keep the current rules?
reason: I am deciding for the service operator, who owns the rules, the contract and the reading of the KPI, but not the regulation. Option 1 can only be adopted by revising the voting quorum, which is a regulation-level change for the regulator. Under K1's process rule it needs an impact statement for A, B, C and the customers. The customer case for option 1 is strong: on-time 121.8 → 131.0 (+9.2, 5/5 seeds), late 10.4 → 1.2, lowest on-time rate 0.84 → 0.98, worst_company_p95_wait_s 273 → 95.6. That is why I do not reject it on its merits. But overriding B's and C's votes now would set a lasting precedent that weakens every company's veto on future amendments. Three costs also remain unexplained: C's utility falls from 28.8 to 19.0 (about a third), B's from 38.9 to 37.2, and road violations rise from 25.8 to 34.0, with unknown safety relevance for other road users. A one-period measurement on 5 seeds is not enough to justify an irreversible change to voting rights while those costs are not understood. I therefore keep v1 and do not follow the recommendation in this period. The vote result (A for, B and C against) stands. The proper next step is a narrowly scoped quorum-revision proposal sent to the regulator with the impact statement, together with measurement of why C loses and which violations increase. Customers keep the current service level for now; this is the cost of this choice and the reason to revisit it soon. Option 2 (hold_limit) is not a substitute: -1.2 on-time, 2/5 seeds.

question: Should option 1 (block_k 3 → 2), which B and C voted against, be adopted by sending a narrowly scoped quorum revision (R1: vote.quorum 2 → 1) to the regulator, or should the rules stay at v1 for this period?
reason:
I am deciding for the service operator, who does not own the regulation. Option 1 can only be adopted by sending R1 (vote.quorum 2 → 1) to the regulator, and I decline to do that in this period, which follows the recommendation.

The customer case is now confirmed in a second period. On-time rises 216.6 → 223.8 (+7.2, 5/5 seeds). Late falls 11.4 → 4.2. The lowest on-time rate rises 0.93 → 0.97. worst_company_p95_wait_s falls 158 → 109. Keeping v1 costs customers about 7.2 on-time deliveries this period, and I record that cost explicitly.

However, R1 is not the narrowly scoped revision D1 contemplated. It is a blanket quorum of 1. That would let any single company pass any future amendment, and it would remove every company's veto, A's included. This is effectively irreversible and could invite strategic amendments.

The costs of option 1 are also still unexplained:
- C's utility falls 65.8 → 56.3 (about 14%).
- B's utility falls 68.5 → 65.5.
- Road violations rise 19.0 → 28.0, and their safety relevance for other road users is unknown.

The period-1 re-measurement (F2.D1.f1) only confirmed reproducibility; it did not diagnose these costs. Option 2 is not a substitute: +0.4 on-time, 2/5 seeds, and C voted against it.

reason:

That condition is not met. vote.quorum is a single value of the constitution, and the measurement row for R1 shows only that 'the vote on proposal(s) 1 changes'. Nothing measured or written shows an instrument that confines a quorum of 1 to one proposal. In force, a quorum of 1 lets any single company pass any rule amendment and removes every company's veto, A's included. That change to the voting structure of the town is hard to reverse.

The customer case is real and I record its cost. Under proposal 1, on-time rises 216.6 -> 223.8 (+7.2, 5/5 seeds) and late falls 11.4 -> 4.2. Next period's demand will resemble this period's normal + rush conditions.

The proposer should look for a different single-parameter change that B and C can accept and that does not raise road violations. block_k 2 may return only if the regulator rules on R2.f1 in its favour.

R2.f1 is the regulator's question, and I do not settle it here. The vote result (A for, B and C against) stands.

question: How to answer the questions due (R2.f1)
How to answer the questions due (R2.f1)
reason:
I am deciding for the regulator. The only option is keep, and this decision answers R2.f1.

Answer to R2.f1, part 1 (scoped quorum): In principle, yes. The regulator would accept a quorum revision confined to amendments that pass every KPI condition on all seeds and do not increase road violations. Such a rule would let customers gain without imposing an unexamined cost on third parties.

Answer to R2.f1, part 2 (can the scope be written): Not with the instrument that exists today. vote.quorum is a single value of the constitution. A change to it applies to every future amendment, and nothing measured or written so far shows a way to condition it on measured outcomes. An amendment of the constitution also moves one parameter by one step. A conditional quorum would need a new kind of constitutional clause, and that is outside what can be proposed or measured now.

The question is also moot for the candidate in hand. block_k 3 -> 2 has raised road violations in every measured period:
- 25.8->34.0
- 19.0->28.0
- 24.2->34.8
- 20.4->29.6
In period 3 it improved only 3/5 seeds. It would not qualify under the scoped rule even if that rule existed.

Answer to R2.f1, part 3 (accept block_k 2 once its violations are shown harmless): Not now. No by-cause breakdown of the violation increase exists, and none is scheduled by anyone in the town. Harmlessness therefore cannot be shown. Even if it were shown, the remaining override path is a blanket quorum cut. That would remove every company's veto on all future amendments in order to pass one rule that B and C have rejected four times. Their utility losses are also unexplained:
- C: 77.7 -> 68.8 in period 4.
- B: 80.3 -> 76.0.
I do not accept that trade.

I record the customer cost. In period 4, customers forgo about 8.0 on-time deliveries (264.6 vs 272.6) and keep 10.0 late deliveries instead of 2.0.

The regulator agrees with D4: the better route is a different single-parameter rule change that B and C can vote for and that does not raise road violations. constitution-v1 with vote.quorum 2 stays in force, and the vote results stand.

The period-4 baseline is reproducible, as the earlier re-measurements were.

title: Shorten hold_limit 60s -> 50s
reason: Release overstays (18.6) and A's and B's blocked time (1172 s and 1024 s) point to long holds at node 8 delaying the worse-served companies. A shorter hold limit aims to cut blocked_s and convert some of B's and A's 7.4 late deliveries into on-time ones. That would raise on_time_deliveries and the floor (B 0.83). It is a different parameter from block_k, as D4 asked, and should not raise evictions. Expected votes: A for and C against, since C's sanctions rise. B is uncertain, because B also waits on the road 25 times but currently incurs no sanctions.
assumptions: Robots respond to a shorter release deadline by leaving node 8 sooner, not only by accruing more Overstay records.
C's long holds are the main source of A's and B's blocked time.
unknowns: Whether hold_limit changes robot behaviour or only the count of Minor violations.

title: Raise sanction_lambda 0.5 -> 1.0
reason: All 12.3 sanction points and most of the 18.6 release overstays fall on C, while A and B absorb about 2200 s of blocking. C's customers stay well served (0.99), so only C's company utility is at stake. If robots do not respond to lambda, the on-time count will not move and the min_improvement gate will reject the proposal.
